chunks.title: Destination postal code not covered by the shipping policy
chunks.text: # Destination postal code not covered by the shipping policy ## Symptom Stock is available and the warehouse-to-dock-to-policy route is valid, yet the fulfillment simulation returns no delivery SLA for one specific postal code. Nearby postal codes may work normally. ## How coverage works Every shipping policy owns a freight table: a list of postal-code ranges (or geographic polygons) with prices and transit times. When the platform prices a delivery it looks up the destination postal code in that table. If no row matches, the policy simply does not serve that destination, and the platform has nothing to offer at checkout. ## How to confirm 1. Identify the shipping policy the dock ships through. 2. Query the freight values for that policy and the destination postal code. An empty result means the destination is not covered. 3. Check that the postal code is written in the platform's canonical format; a missing hyphen or leading zero can fall outside every range. ## Recommended action

chunks.title: Linking loading docks to shipping policies
chunks.text: # Linking loading docks to shipping policies A route from a dock to a shipping policy exists only when both sides agree: - the dock lists the policy's freight table among its freight table ids, and - the policy lists the dock among its linked docks. ## Why both sides matter Dock and policy records are edited independently. A dock can keep a stale freight table id after a policy is deleted or recreated, and a policy can be linked to a dock that was later reconfigured. Trusting only one side can make a route look valid when the platform will not use it. ## How to verify 1. Read the dock: is it active, and which freight table ids does it list? 2. For each id, read the shipping policy: is it active, and does it list this dock back? 3. A dock with no active, mutually linked policy has no route. ## Common mistakes - Policy deactivated for maintenance and never reactivated. - Policy cloned to create a new carrier contract, but the dock still points at the old one. - Dock linked to a policy

chunks.title: When to escalate an investigation to a specialist
chunks.text: # When to escalate an investigation to a specialist The investigator only issues a finding when every piece of required evidence was collected and agrees. In all other cases it stops and asks for a human. ## Escalate when - **Required intake is missing**: SKU, quantity, seller or destination postal code is unknown or unconfirmed. Complete the intake first. - **A required check failed**: a lookup was denied, timed out or returned an unexpected payload. - **Evidence is insufficient**: not every step of the route could be observed. - **Evidence is contradictory**: the symptom could not be reproduced, or an upstream step failed. - **The case is unsupported**: the problem is outside the supported findings, such as payment disputes or carrier delays. ## How to hand off Attach the evidence ledger, not a summary of it. chunks.title: Finding gaps in freight table postal-code ranges
chunks.text: # Finding gaps in freight table postal-code ranges Freight tables are maintained as postal-code ranges, often imported from a carrier spreadsheet. Gaps appear when ranges are trimmed, when a carrier stops serving a region, or when two imports overlap and one is deleted. ## Typical signs - A single neighbourhood or city fails while the surrounding region works. - Failures started right after a freight table import. - The same SKU ships fine to a nearby postal code through the same dock. ## How to locate the gap 1. Export the policy's freight table and sort the rows by range start. 2. Walk the rows and look for an end value followed by a start value that is more than one postal code away. 3. Compare the gap with the destinations reported in tickets. 4. Check whether a polygon entry was meant to cover the area instead of a numeric range. ## Fixing it Add a range that closes the gap, with the carrier's price and transit time for that area. chunks.title: Reading a fulfillment simulation result
chunks.text: # Reading a fulfillment simulation result A fulfillment simulation asks the platform "if this customer bought this SKU, in this quantity, from this seller, delivered to this postal code, what would checkout offer?". It does not create an order and has no side effects. ## Inputs SKU id, quantity, seller id and destination postal code. chunks.title: Reserved, available and unlimited inventory
chunks.text: # Reserved, available and unlimited inventory Each warehouse reports three numbers for a SKU: - **quantity**: units physically recorded in the warehouse. - **reserved quantity**: units held by orders that are placed but not yet shipped. - **unlimited quantity flag**: the SKU is made to order or dropshipped and never runs out. ## Usable stock Usable stock is quantity minus reserved quantity, unless the unlimited flag is set. A SKU with quantity 10 and reserved 10 shows stock in back-office screens but is not sellable. Many "stock is there but I cannot buy it" tickets are reservations, not logistics problems. ## Investigation tips - Compare the requested quantity with usable stock in each warehouse, not the total across warehouses. An order is fulfilled from one warehouse route at a time. - Reservations normally release when an order is cancelled or after the payment window expires. Long-lived reservations point to stuck orders. - An inventory read that is denied is a permission problem;

chunks.title: Invoicing and shipment tracking
chunks.text: # Invoicing and shipment tracking ## Invoicing An order is invoiced when the seller issues the fiscal invoice and attaches it to the order's package. The package then carries the invoice number and value. Invoicing is usually the moment the order leaves the seller's hands and is collected by the carrier. Common invoicing problems: - invoice value different from the order total because of a partial shipment; - invoice attached to the wrong package in a multi-package order; - order stuck in handling because the seller's ERP integration failed to post the invoice. ## Tracking After invoicing, the carrier's tracking events are attached to the package. A courier status marked as finished means the carrier reported delivery. ## Investigating "where is my order?" 1. Confirm the order is invoiced; before that there is nothing to track. 2. chunks.title: Cancelling an order
chunks.text: # Cancelling an order Who can cancel and how depends on the order status. ## Before invoicing Until the order is invoiced, the seller, the marketplace operator or the customer (within the self-service window) can request cancellation. The platform releases the reserved inventory and voids or refunds the payment automatically. ## After invoicing Once an invoice exists, a plain cancellation is no longer possible. The package may already be with the carrier, and the fiscal document must be reversed. Handle these cases as a return: see "Processing returns and refunds". ## What support should check - Current status and whether an invoice was issued. - Payment status: a denied payment usually leads to automatic cancellation without any manual step. - Whether the customer request arrived inside the self-service window. ## What support should not do The investigator never cancels orders. chunks.title: Order status lifecycle
chunks.text: # Order status lifecycle Orders move through a fixed sequence of statuses. Knowing the current status tells support which actions are still possible. 1. **Order placed**: the customer finished checkout. 2. **Payment pending**: waiting for the payment provider. 3. **Payment approved** or **payment denied**: a denied payment stops the flow and usually leads to cancellation. 4. **Ready for handling**: the seller can start picking and packing. 5. **Handling**: items are being prepared. 6. **Invoiced**: the fiscal invoice was issued and the package handed to the carrier. 7. **Cancelled**: terminal; no further transitions. ## Reading the history The order's status history lists each transition with a timestamp. Long gaps between two statuses are the first thing to look at when a customer says an order is "stuck". chunks.title: Read access denied during an investigation
chunks.text: # Read access denied during an investigation Investigations use read-only credentials. Sometimes a lookup is rejected with a permission error (HTTP 403) instead of returning data. Typical causes: - the order belongs to another seller account than the one support has access to; - the credential's role lacks read access to logistics configuration (warehouses, docks or shipping policies); - a credential was rotated and the old one revoked. ## Why it matters A denied read is not the same as "not found". A missing order is a normal answer; a permission error means the evidence could not be collected at all. The investigator must never treat a denied read as proof that something does not exist, and must not guess the missing evidence. ## What to do 1. Note which capability was denied and for which id. 2. chunks.title: Processing returns and refunds
chunks.text: # Processing returns and refunds A return applies to an order that was already invoiced. It reverses the goods flow and, separately, the money flow. ## Steps 1. The customer or the seller opens a return request listing the items and the reason. 2. The seller approves the request and issues return shipping instructions. 3. The returned items are received and inspected at the warehouse. 4. The seller issues the return fiscal document and triggers the refund. 5. The refund goes back to the original payment method; timing depends on the payment provider. ## Partial returns Only some items or some quantities may be returned. The refund covers the returned items plus any proportional shipping the seller policy allows. ## Support checklist - Is the order invoiced? If not, it is a cancellation, not a return. - Is the request inside the return window? - Has the warehouse received the goods? Refunds normally wait for receipt. chunks.title: Shipping policies priced by a runtime rate provider
chunks.text: # Shipping policies priced by a runtime rate provider Some docks do not rely on a static freight table. Instead they name a runtime rate provider: an integration that computes coverage and price at checkout time, for example for polygon-based delivery areas, same-day couriers or external carrier quotes. ## What this means for investigations When a dock names a runtime rate provider, the static freight table does not tell the whole story. An empty freight lookup does not prove the destination is uncovered, because the provider may answer differently at request time. The read-only investigator therefore cannot establish a deterministic route for such docks and must not issue a coverage finding. ## How to proceed 1. Note that the dock uses a runtime rate provider. 2. Check the provider's own status page or logs for errors around the ticket time. 3. Ask the provider team whether the destination is inside their service area. 4. Escalate to a specialist if the provider cannot be checked from

chunks.title: Product in stock but no delivery options at checkout
chunks.text: # Product in stock but no delivery options at checkout ## Symptom A shopper adds a SKU to the cart, the product page shows it as available, but checkout offers no shipping method for their address. Support tickets usually read "the item has stock but no delivery option shows up" or "frete indisponível". ## Why it happens Availability and deliverability are decided by different parts of the platform. Inventory only answers "is there usable quantity in some warehouse?". A delivery option additionally needs a complete logistics route: the warehouse holding the stock must be mapped to a loading dock, the dock must ship through an active shipping policy, and that policy's freight table must cover the destination postal code. If any link is missing, the fulfillment simulation returns the item as available with an empty list of delivery SLAs. ## How to investigate 1. chunks.title: Mapping warehouses to loading docks
chunks.text: # Mapping warehouses to loading docks A warehouse holds inventory; a loading dock is where shipments leave. The platform only creates delivery options for stock in a warehouse that is linked to at least one active dock. ## What to check - The warehouse record is active. - The warehouse lists one or more docks in its dock mapping. - Each mapped dock is itself active. A warehouse with stock but no dock mapping produces "available" items with no delivery option. This often happens when a new warehouse is created and stock is loaded before logistics finishes the configuration. ## Several docks per warehouse When a warehouse maps to more than one dock, a platform may rank the docks by processing time, cost overhead or a manual priority. The investigator does not reproduce that ranking: it follows the first dock the warehouse reports and treats the route as observed only for that dock.
